cards.front: A {{c1::population}} is all the members of one species living in the same place.
cards.quote: a population, all the members of one species living in the same place
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: What is the rule for how the size of a population changes?
cards.back: Populations rise when additions exceed losses, and fall when losses exceed additions.
cards.quote: Populations rise when additions exceed losses, and fall when losses exceed additions.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: In the additions-and-losses rule for a population, what counts as additions and what counts as losses?
cards.back: Additions are births and arrivals. Losses are deaths and departures.
cards.quote: Here, additions mean births and arrivals; losses mean deaths and departures.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: Does the additions-and-losses rule tell you which factor caused a population to change? Explain.
cards.back: No. The rule tells how the number changes over a chosen time, not which factor caused the change.
cards.quote: Scope: the rule tells how the number changes over a chosen time, not which factor caused the change.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: The Chesapeake Bay winter survey estimated 367 million blue crabs in 1991–1992 and 852 million in 1992–1993. By how much did the estimate change, and about how many times its old size is the new estimate?
cards.back: 852 − 367 = 485 million more crabs. 852 ÷ 367 is about 2.32, so the estimate rose to about 2.32 times its size.
cards.quote: For the survey, the estimate rose by 485 million crabs, to about 2.32 times its size.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: A {{c1::limiting factor}} is anything that keeps a population from growing larger.
cards.quote: A limiting factor is anything that keeps a population from growing larger.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: What is the difference between a biotic factor and an abiotic factor? Give one example of each.
cards.back: A biotic factor is a living part of the environment, such as predators, food or grass. An abiotic factor is a nonliving part, such as temperature or salt in the water.
cards.quote: An abiotic factor is a nonliving part of the environment, such as temperature or salt in the water.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: How does a very cold winter act as a limiting factor on blue crabs?
cards.back: It is an abiotic factor. More crabs die before spring, which increases losses.
cards.quote: More crabs die before spring, increasing losses.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: Why can shallow water and grass lower the losses of young blue crabs?
cards.back: They give hiding places, which protect young crabs from big crabs.
cards.quote: Hiding places can lower losses by protecting young crabs from big crabs.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: In a cove, the patch of underwater grass becomes smaller. Predict what happens to young crabs, and name the idea that explains it.
cards.back: Some young crabs find cover and others are left exposed and may be eaten, so losses of young crabs rise. This is competition for a limited hiding place.
cards.quote: With a smaller patch of grass, some young crabs find cover, and others are left exposed and may be eaten.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: Lab tests suggest that cold limits how far north blue crabs can survive. If northern winters stay milder for many years, what could happen to the crab's range, and what evidence would show it really happened?
cards.back: Crabs could live farther north. Lab tests alone cannot show the move has happened; that takes field records of crabs found farther north over many years.
cards.quote: Lab tests suggest that cold limits how far north blue crabs can survive.
cards.section: Explain: what makes a population grow or shrink

cards.front: In the model crab cove, grass is high, winters are mild and harvest is off. Then only year 4 is made harsh. What happens to the bars for year 4 and the years after it?
cards.back: The year 4 bar drops because the harsh winter raises deaths that year. Year 5 is lower than in the all-mild run but higher than year 4, and later bars climb back toward the earlier level in this model.
cards.why: A real population does not always recover.
cards.quote: The year 4 bar drops, because the harsh winter raises deaths that year.
cards.section: Explore: run a crab cove for ten years

cards.front: Why does a wildfire not always end a pine forest for good?
cards.back: In some pine forests, heat opens cones and drops seeds, so new trees start. After very hot fires elsewhere, few trees were left to drop seeds, and the forest may not return.
cards.quote: In some pine forests, the heat also opens cones and drops seeds, so new trees start.
cards.section: Explain: natural causes and human causes

cards.front: A flood pushes crabs out of a cove, but they all survive. Which loss increased, deaths or departures?
cards.back: Departures increased. Deaths did not, because the crabs survived.
cards.quote: Departures increased. Deaths did not, because the crabs survived.
cards.section: Explain: natural causes and human causes

cards.front: In a study, adult coho salmon were placed in untreated rain runoff from a busy Seattle road, and others in the same runoff after it flowed through soil. What happened, and what does it show about pollution?
cards.back: All the coho in untreated runoff died within 24 hours; all 20 in the soil-filtered runoff survived. Pollution can raise deaths, and in this study, runoff that flowed through soil did not kill the coho.
cards.quote: In the study, all of the adult coho salmon placed in untreated rain runoff from a busy Seattle road died within 24 hours.
cards.section: The coho salmon runoff study

cards.front: {{c1::Overharvesting}} means people catch or collect a species faster than it can replace itself.
cards.quote: Overharvesting means people catch or collect a species faster than it can replace itself.
cards.section: Explain: natural causes and human causes

cards.front: Taking only as many as the population can replace, so it lasts, is called {{c1::sustainable}} harvest.
cards.quote: This is sustainable harvest: taking only as many as the population can replace, so it lasts.
cards.section: Explain: limits that help a population recover

cards.front: Why did Virginia and Maryland limit the catch of female blue crabs in particular?
cards.back: Females carry the eggs, so leaving more of them can mean more young crabs later.
cards.quote: Females carry the eggs, so leaving more of them can mean more young crabs later.
cards.section: Explain: limits that help a population recover

cards.front: Why do managers keep counting crabs after they set harvest limits?
cards.back: A limit is not a promise. Harvest limits can reduce one loss and leave more adults to reproduce, but recovery is not certain.
cards.quote: A limit is not a promise, so managers keep counting.
cards.section: Explain: limits that help a population recover

cards.front: Crabbers catch most of the adult female blue crabs every year for many years. Predict what happens to young crabs and to the population.
cards.back: Fewer young crabs are born, and the numbers may keep falling. Females carry the eggs, so removing most of them raises losses and cuts additions.
cards.quote: Virginia and Maryland set a plan to catch about 34 percent fewer female crabs than in 2004 to 2007.
cards.section: Explain: limits that help a population recover

cards.front: Why is the winter survey's young-crab number not a direct count of births in the Bay?
cards.back: Young crabs make a round trip: larvae drift out to sea and young crabs later move back in. So the number also depends on how many larvae survive at sea and return.
cards.quote: So the survey's young-crab number is not a direct count of births.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the winter crab survey

cards.front: New limits on female harvest began in spring 2008. From winter 2007–2008 to 2011–2012 the Bay survey total rose from 293 to 765 million, while adult females rose only from 91 to 95 million. Do these numbers show the limits alone caused the rise?
cards.back: No. The total rose by 472 million but adult females by only 4 million. Most of the later total was young crabs, and many factors affect young crabs, so the table cannot show one cause.
cards.quote: Most of the later total was young crabs, so the table does not show that the female-harvest limits alone caused the rise.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the winter crab survey

cards.front: In the Bay survey, the total was 238 million in 2024–2025 and 349 million in 2025–2026. Adult females were 108 million and 81 million. Did the total and adult females move in the same direction?
cards.back: No. The total rose by 111 million; adult females fell by 27 million. Different parts of a population can move in different directions.
cards.quote: Different parts of a population can move in different directions.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the winter crab survey

cards.front: Adult females in the Bay survey fell from 108 to 81 million in 2025–2026, and Maryland reported a cold winter. Name a limiting factor that could fit, and say why the table cannot prove it.
cards.back: A cold winter is an abiotic factor that can raise deaths; Maryland reported about 12 percent of adult females died. But the table gives counts, not causes, so a survey pattern does not prove one cause.
cards.quote: Maryland reported that about 12 percent of adult females died during the cold winter of 2025–2026.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the winter crab survey

cards.front: Plan a fair test of whether dish soap in water changes how a duckweed population grows. Name the independent variable, dependent variable and control.
cards.back: Independent: soap in the pond water, for example 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 milliliters per liter. Dependent: number of fronds counted every two days for two weeks. Control: cups with no soap. Keep water, cup, light, temperature and 10 starting fronds the same, with four cups per level.
cards.quote: Independent variable: soap mixed into the pond water before filling the cups, for example 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 milliliters per liter.
cards.section: Design problem
